title: Red Lentil Dal with Cumin-Garlic Tadka
description: Split red lentils simmer into a soft, golden stew in about 25 minutes, then get a hot pour of cumin, garlic, and onion fried in oil. Over rice, it comes to about $1 a bowl.
notes: Red lentils cook quickly and break down into a thick, creamy stew; brown or green lentils take 35 to 45 minutes and stay whole, which is also fine. Ghee in place of the oil gives a richer tadka but adds milk and makes the dish no longer vegan or dairy-free. A cup of frozen peas or two handfuls of baby spinach can go in for the last 5 minutes of simmering. The dal thickens as it sits; loosen it with hot water when you reheat. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and keep them up to 4 days, or freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat to 165°F, stirring, before serving.

ingredients.name: dried split red lentils (300 g), rinsed until the water runs clear
cooked brown or white rice, for serving

instructions: Combine the lentils, water, turmeric, and tomato paste in a large saucepan. Bring to a boil over high heat, skim off any foam, then reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer, partly covered and stirring now and then, for 20 to 25 minutes, until the lentils have collapsed and the pot looks like a thick soup. Stir in 1 teaspoon of the salt.

While the lentils simmer, make the tadka. Heat the oil in a small skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 20 to 30 seconds, until fragrant and a shade darker.
Add the onion, reduce the heat to medium, and cook, stirring often, for 6 to 8 minutes, until soft and golden at the edges.
Stir in the garlic, ginger, coriander, and red pepper flakes and cook for about 1 minute, until the garlic is just turning golden. Do not let it brown or it will taste bitter.

Scrape the tadka, oil and all, into the lentils. Stir well and simmer for 5 minutes more so the flavors come together. If the dal is thicker than you like, stir in hot water a few tablespoons at a time; it will thicken again as it stands.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the lemon juice. Taste and add the remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt if it needs it. Spoon over the rice and scatter with cilantro.

title: Rajma (Punjabi-Style Kidney Bean Curry) with Basmati Rice
description: Canned kidney beans simmer in a slow-cooked onion, ginger, and tomato masala until the gravy clings to every bean. Spooned over basmati rice, this Punjabi comfort meal runs about $1.25 a plate.
notes: The deeply golden onion is the whole flavor base, so give it the full 10 to 12 minutes. To cut the cost further, soak 1 cup (200 g) dried kidney beans overnight, then boil them in fresh water for about 1 hour until fully tender before adding them in place of the canned beans; dried kidney beans must be fully cooked, never eaten soaked and raw. A spoonful of plain yogurt on the side is traditional but adds milk. Rajma tastes better the next day as the beans soak up the gravy. Refrigerate within 2 hours; the curry keeps 4 days in the refrigerator and freezes well for 3 months, while the rice is best kept separately and used within 3 days. Reheat everything to 165°F, adding a splash of water to the curry.

ingredients.name: basmati rice (300 g), rinsed until the water runs mostly clear
kidney beans (15 oz each), drained and rinsed

instructions: Start the rice. Combine the rice, 2 1/4 cups water, and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt in a medium saucepan and bring to a boil over high heat. Cover, reduce the heat to the lowest setting, and cook for 15 minutes. Take it off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes, then fluff with a fork.

Heat the oil in a Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the cumin seeds and sizzle for 20 seconds, then add the onion. Reduce the heat to medium and cook, stirring often, for 10 to 12 minutes, until the onion is soft and deeply golden brown.
Stir in the garlic and ginger and cook for 1 minute, then add the coriander, turmeric, and cayenne and stir for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the crushed tomatoes and cook, stirring often, for 6 to 8 minutes, until the mixture is thick and paste-like and oil beads at the edges.

Add the beans, 1 1/2 cups water, and the remaining 1 teaspoon salt. Bring to a simmer, then cook partly covered over medium-low heat for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally and mashing a few spoonfuls of beans against the side of the pot to thicken the gravy. It should coat the beans but still be spoonable; add a little water if it gets too thick.
Stir in the garam masala and cilantro and taste for salt. Serve the rajma over the rice.

title: Egg Curry in Onion-Tomato Masala
description: Hard-boiled eggs, briefly fried with turmeric, then simmered in a spiced onion and tomato gravy with a splash of coconut milk. Eight eggs feed four over rice for about $1.50 a plate.
notes: Frying the peeled eggs with turmeric gives them blistered golden spots and a skin that holds the gravy; skip it if you are short on time and simply add the eggs at the end. The coconut milk rounds out the heat; leave it out and use an extra 1/2 cup water for a sharper, leaner curry. Ghee in place of the oil is traditional but adds milk. Boiled eggs for later meals keep 1 week in the refrigerator in their shells. Refrigerate the curry within 2 hours and use within 3 days; it does not freeze well because the egg whites turn rubbery. Reheat gently to 165°F, covered, so the eggs warm through without overcooking.

ingredients.name: cooked brown or white rice, for serving

instructions: Put the eggs in a medium saucepan, cover with cold water by an inch, and bring to a boil over high heat. Cover, take the pan off the heat, and let stand 11 minutes. Move the eggs to a bowl of ice water for 5 minutes, then peel and pat dry.

Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat. Add the eggs with 1/4 teaspoon of the turmeric and 1/4 teaspoon of the salt and fry, turning with a spoon, for 2 to 3 minutes, until they have golden blistered spots. Move them to a plate.
Add the remaining 2 tablespoons oil and the onion to the skillet. Cook over medium heat, stirring often, for 8 to 10 minutes, until soft and golden.
Stir in the garlic and ginger and cook 1 minute, then add the cumin, coriander, cayenne, and the remaining 1/4 teaspoon turmeric and stir for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the crushed tomatoes and the remaining 1 teaspoon salt. Cook, stirring often, for 6 to 8 minutes, until the masala is thick and oil beads at the edges.

Pour in the water and coconut milk, bring to a simmer, and cook for 5 minutes, until the gravy is the thickness of a thin tomato soup. Return the eggs, spoon gravy over them, cover, and simmer gently for 5 minutes to heat them through.
Stir in the garam masala and cilantro, taste for salt, and serve over the rice, two eggs per person.

title: Spanish Tortilla (Potato and Onion Omelet)
description: Tender slices of potato and sweet onion set in eggs, cooked slowly in a skillet and flipped once. Eight eggs and a few potatoes make dinner for four at about $1.25 a wedge, warm or at room temperature.
equipment: large flat plate or pot lid wider than the skillet
notes: The potatoes should poach in the oil at a lazy bubble rather than fry, so lower the heat if they start to brown. Strain and refrigerate the leftover oil; it is good for the next tortilla or for roasting vegetables within 2 weeks. If you are nervous about the flip, cook the first side as directed, then slide the skillet under a broiler for 2 to 3 minutes until the top is set. A spoonful of mayonnaise or a few roasted red peppers on the side are classic. The tortilla is cooked when the center reaches 160°F. Refrigerate within 2 hours and keep up to 3 days; eat cold, at room temperature within 2 hours of taking it out, or reheat to 165°F. It does not freeze well because the potatoes turn grainy.

ingredients.name: russet or yukon gold potatoes, peeled, halved lengthwise, and sliced 1/8 inch thick
large yellow onion, halved and thinly sliced

instructions: Heat the oil in a 10-inch nonstick skillet over medium heat. Add the potatoes, onion, and 3/4 teaspoon of the salt and stir to coat. Cook, stirring every few minutes and adjusting the heat so the oil barely bubbles without browning anything, for 20 to 25 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and break easily when pressed with a spoon.
Set a colander over a large bowl and drain the potatoes and onion, reserving the oil. Let them cool for 5 minutes.

In another large bowl, whisk the eggs with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt and several grinds of pepper. Fold in the warm potatoes and onion and let the mixture sit for 5 minutes so the potatoes soak up some egg.

Wipe out the skillet and heat 2 tablespoons of the reserved oil over medium-high heat until shimmering. Pour in the egg mixture and spread it level. Cook for 1 minute, then reduce the heat to medium-low. Run a spatula around the edge, tucking it under to round the sides, and cook for 6 to 8 minutes, until the edges are set, the bottom is golden, and the center is wobbly but no longer liquid.

Place a large flat plate over the skillet. Holding the plate firmly with a kitchen towel, flip the skillet and plate together in one motion so the tortilla lands on the plate. Add 1 tablespoon of the reserved oil to the skillet and slide the tortilla back in, uncooked side down, tucking the edges under with the spatula.

Cook for 3 to 5 minutes more, until the center is just set; a thermometer in the middle should read 160°F and a knife should come out with only a little moist egg. Slide onto a cutting board and let rest 10 minutes.
Cut into wedges and serve warm or at room temperature with the greens alongside.

title: Cuban-Style Black Beans and Rice
description: Black beans stewed with a sofrito of onion, green pepper, garlic, cumin, and oregano, finished with a little vinegar and spooned over white rice. Two cans feed six at under $1 a bowl.
notes: Using the liquid from the cans gives the beans body; if your cans are heavily salted, drain one and add 1/2 cup more water. For the lowest cost, cook 1 pound of dried black beans from scratch (soak overnight, simmer 1 to 1 1/2 hours until tender), which makes about twice this amount for the same price as the cans. Apple cider vinegar works in place of red wine vinegar. A fried egg on top makes a bigger meal but adds eggs. Refrigerate within 2 hours; the beans keep 4 days and freeze for 3 months, and the rice keeps 3 days. Reheat to 165°F with a splash of water.

ingredients.name: long grain white rice (370 g), rinsed
black beans (15 oz each), not drained
lime, cut into wedges, for serving

instructions: Combine the rice, 3 cups water, and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt in a medium saucepan and bring to a boil over high heat. Cover, reduce the heat to the lowest setting, and cook for 15 minutes. Take it off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes, then fluff with a fork.
Meanwhile, heat the oil in a Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the onion, bell pepper, and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt and cook, stirring often, for 8 to 10 minutes, until very soft but not browned.
Stir in the garlic, cumin, and oregano and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.

Add the beans with their liquid, 1/2 cup water, the bay leaf, and the sugar. Bring to a simmer and cook uncovered over medium-low heat for 20 minutes, stirring now and then and mashing about 1/2 cup of the beans against the side of the pot, until the liquid is glossy and thick enough to coat a spoon.
Discard the bay leaf. Stir in the vinegar, the remaining 3/4 teaspoon salt, and pepper to taste, and simmer 2 minutes more. Taste; it should be savory with a faint tang.
Spoon the beans over the rice and top with cilantro and a squeeze of lime.

title: Atakilt Wat (Ethiopian-Inspired Cabbage, Carrots, and Potatoes)
description: Cabbage, carrots, and potatoes braise in their own steam with onion, garlic, ginger, and turmeric until the cabbage is silky and the potatoes are soft. A full pot costs under $1 a serving.
notes: This is a mild dish by design; the jalapeño adds a gentle warmth and can be left out or doubled. Ethiopian cooks often use niter kibbeh, a spiced clarified butter, in place of the oil, which is delicious but adds milk. The pot will look overfull when the cabbage goes in; it collapses to a third of its volume within minutes. Serve with injera if you can find it, or with rice or flatbread, and pair it with a lentil stew for a fuller plate. Refrigerate within 2 hours and keep up to 4 days; it freezes for 2 months, though the cabbage softens further. Reheat to 165°F in a covered pan with a splash of water.

ingredients.name: large yellow onion, halved and thinly sliced
carrot, peeled and cut into 2-inch sticks (about 3/4 lb)
russet or yukon gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 1 1/2-inch chunks
green cabbage, cored and cut into 1-inch-wide strips (about half a large head)
cooked brown or white rice, for serving

instructions: Heat the oil in a large Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the onion and 1/4 teaspoon of the salt and cook, stirring often, for 8 minutes, until soft and lightly golden.
Stir in the garlic, ginger, turmeric, cumin, and cardamom and cook for 1 minute, until the oil turns deep yellow and smells fragrant.
Add the carrots, potatoes, 1/2 teaspoon of the salt, and the water. Stir to coat, cover, and cook over medium-low heat for 10 minutes, stirring once.

Pile the cabbage on top, sprinkle with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt, and lay the jalapeño halves on top. Cover and cook for 5 minutes, until the cabbage has wilted enough to stir, then fold it down into the vegetables below.

Cover again and cook for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes and adding a splash of water if the bottom looks dry, until the potatoes are tender when pierced and the cabbage is silky and golden from the turmeric.
Season with pepper, taste for salt, and remove the jalapeño if you prefer. Serve hot over rice.

title: Japanese-Inspired Tofu and Potato Simmer (Nikujaga Style)
description: Pan-browned tofu, potatoes, carrots, and onion simmer in a sweet-salty tamari and mirin broth until the potatoes soak it up, the way nikujaga is made with beef. With rice, about $1.50 a bowl.
equipment: wide Dutch oven or 12-inch deep skillet with lid
notes: Pressing the tofu for 15 minutes between paper towels under a heavy plate lets it brown instead of steam; for a crisper edge, toss the cubes in 1 tablespoon cornstarch before frying. Regular low-sodium soy sauce can stand in for the tamari but adds wheat, so the dish would no longer be gluten-free. Frozen green beans or a handful of sliced mushrooms can go in with the potatoes. The broth is meant to be light and plentiful; spoon some over the rice. Refrigerate within 2 hours and keep up to 3 days; it does not freeze well because the potatoes turn grainy. Reheat to 165°F, covered, over low heat.

ingredients.name: japanese short-grain rice (300 g), rinsed until the water runs mostly clear
extra-firm tofu, drained, pressed 15 minutes, and cut into 1-inch cubes
large yellow onion, cut into 1/2-inch wedges
carrot, peeled and cut into 1/2-inch chunks
russet or yukon gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 1 1/2-inch chunks
fresh ginger, cut into thin matchsticks

instructions: Put the rice and 1 3/4 cups water in a medium saucepan and let it soak for 20 minutes while you prepare the vegetables. Bring to a boil over high heat, cover, reduce the heat to the lowest setting, and cook for 13 minutes. Take it off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes.

Pat the tofu cubes dry and sprinkle with the salt. Heat the oil in a wide Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the tofu in a single layer and cook without moving for 3 to 4 minutes, until golden underneath, then turn and brown a second side, 3 minutes more. Move the tofu to a plate.

Add the onion and carrots to the pot and cook, stirring, for 3 minutes, until the onion starts to soften. Add the potatoes, broth, tamari, mirin, sugar, and ginger, scraping up any browned bits, and bring to a boil.

Reduce the heat to a gentle simmer and cover with the lid slightly ajar. Cook for 18 to 20 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the potatoes are tender when pierced with a knife but still hold their shape.

Return the tofu to the pot and add the peas. Simmer uncovered for 5 minutes so the broth reduces a little and the tofu warms through. Taste the broth; it should be sweet and savory, and a pinch more salt is fine if it tastes flat.
Fluff the rice and divide among bowls. Spoon the tofu, vegetables, and plenty of broth over the top and scatter with scallions.

title: Pinto Bean Enfrijoladas with Chipotle
description: Warm corn tortillas dipped in a smooth, smoky pinto bean sauce, folded, and topped with red onion, cilantro, and lime. Two cans of beans and a dozen tortillas make dinner for four at about $1.25 a plate.
notes: Black beans work just as well as pinto. One chipotle gives a mild, smoky heat; use two for a spicier sauce or leave it out for children and add 1/2 teaspoon smoked paprika instead. Crumbled feta or queso fresco on top is traditional but adds milk, and a fried egg on top adds eggs. The sauce should be the thickness of thin pancake batter so it coats the tortillas without soaking through them. Store leftover sauce separately; it keeps 4 days refrigerated and freezes for 3 months, and it doubles as a soup thinned with broth. Assembled enfrijoladas soften as they sit, so refrigerate within 2 hours, eat within 2 days, and reheat to 165°F covered in a skillet with a spoonful of sauce.

ingredients.name: pinto beans (15 oz each), drained and rinsed
chipotle peppers in adobo, plus 2 teaspoons of the sauce
medium red onions, thinly sliced, for serving
lime, cut into wedges, for serving

instructions: Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Add the yellow onion and cook, stirring, for 5 minutes, until soft. Stir in the garlic, cumin, and oregano and cook 1 minute, until fragrant.
Add the beans, chipotle and its sauce, broth, and salt. Bring to a simmer and cook for 10 minutes so the beans soften and the flavors blend.

Blend the mixture until completely smooth. If using a countertop blender, fill it no more than halfway, remove the center cap of the lid, and cover with a folded towel so steam can escape. Return the sauce to the pan and keep it warm over low heat; it should pour like thin pancake batter, so stir in broth a tablespoon at a time if it is thicker.

Heat a 10-inch skillet over medium-high heat and brush with a little of the remaining oil. Warm the tortillas one or two at a time for about 30 seconds per side, until soft and pliable, and stack them under a clean towel as you go.

Working with one tortilla at a time, use tongs to dip it into the warm sauce so both sides are coated, then fold it in half and in half again into a wedge. Lay three overlapping wedges on each plate and spoon a little extra sauce over the top.
Scatter the red onion and cilantro over the plates, add avocado slices if using, and serve right away with lime wedges for squeezing.

title: Tuscan-Style White Beans and Kale on Garlic Toast
description: Cannellini beans and kale stewed with garlic, rosemary, and olive oil until brothy and soft, ladled over thick garlic-rubbed toast. Two cans of beans and a bunch of kale make four bowls for about $1.50 each.
notes: Collard greens, Swiss chard, or green cabbage can replace the kale; collards need about 10 minutes more simmering. A shower of grated parmesan on top is classic but adds milk. Use a gluten-free loaf, or skip the toast and serve over rice, to make the dish gluten-free. The bean liquid from the cans gives the broth body; if you prefer, drain the beans and use 1/2 cup more vegetable broth. Day-old bread toasts better than fresh. Refrigerate the beans within 2 hours and keep up to 4 days, or freeze for 3 months; make the toast fresh each time. Reheat the beans to 165°F with a splash of broth or water.

ingredients.name: extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for drizzling
garlic, 5 thinly sliced and 1 left whole
lacinato or curly kale (about 10 oz), stems removed, leaves torn into 2-inch pieces
cannellini beans (15 oz each), not drained
stale crusty country bread, cut 1 inch thick

instructions: Heat the oil in a Dutch oven over medium-low heat. Add the sliced garlic and red pepper flakes and cook, stirring, for 2 to 3 minutes, until the garlic is barely golden and fragrant; do not let it brown.
Add the onion, rosemary sprig, and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt. Raise the heat to medium and cook, stirring often, for 6 to 8 minutes, until the onion is soft.
Add the kale a few handfuls at a time with 1/4 teaspoon of the salt, stirring until each addition wilts before adding more, about 4 minutes in all.

Pour in the beans with their liquid and the broth. Bring to a simmer and cook partly covered over medium-low heat for 15 minutes, mashing about 1/2 cup of the beans against the side of the pot to thicken the broth, until the kale is tender and silky.

While the beans simmer, toast the bread under the broiler or in a dry 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat until golden on both sides, 2 to 3 minutes per side. Rub one side of each slice with the whole garlic clove, drizzle with olive oil, and sprinkle with the remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt.

Remove the rosemary sprig, stir in the lemon juice, and season with pepper. Taste for salt. Set a slice of toast in each shallow bowl, ladle the beans and broth over it, and finish with a drizzle of olive oil.

title: Korean-Inspired Vegetable Pancakes (Yachaejeon)
description: Crisp-edged, chewy pancakes packed with scallions, carrot, and cabbage in a thin flour-and-cornstarch batter, served with a soy-vinegar dipping sauce. A whole batch costs about $3, well under $1 a serving.
notes: The batter should be thin, like heavy cream, and ice-cold water keeps the pancakes crisp rather than bready; mix just until smooth. Any firm vegetable cut thin works: zucchini, frozen corn, thinly sliced mushrooms, or a handful of chopped kimchi in place of the cabbage. For a gluten-free version, use a gluten-free flour blend and gluten-free tamari in the sauce. Leftover pancakes keep 3 days in the refrigerator and 2 months in the freezer layered between parchment; reheat them in a dry skillet over medium heat so they crisp again, since the microwave makes them soft. Refrigerate within 2 hours and reheat to 165°F. Serve two pancakes as a main with rice and a quick cucumber salad, or cut them small as an appetizer.

ingredients.name: scallion, thinly sliced, for the sauce
scallion, cut into 2-inch lengths, thick white parts halved lengthwise
large carrot, cut into thin matchsticks
green cabbage, very thinly sliced (about 1/4 small head)

instructions: Make the dipping sauce by stirring together the soy sauce, rice vinegar, sesame oil, sesame seeds, sugar, red pepper flakes, and the sliced scallion in a small bowl. Set aside.
In a large bowl, whisk the flour, cornstarch, and salt. Add the ice-cold water and whisk just until smooth; the batter should be thin, about the thickness of heavy cream. Do not overmix.
Fold in the scallion lengths, carrot, cabbage, and onion. The mixture should look like vegetables lightly held together by batter rather than batter with some vegetables in it.

Heat 2 tablespoons of the oil in a 10-inch skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add half the vegetable mixture and spread it into a thin, even round with a spatula, pressing lightly. Cook for 4 to 5 minutes, until the bottom is deeply golden and crisp and the edges look lacy; lift an edge to check.

Flip the pancake with a wide spatula, or slide it onto a plate and invert it back into the pan. Drizzle 1 tablespoon more oil around the edges, press the pancake flat, and cook for 3 to 4 minutes, until the second side is golden and crisp. Move it to a wire rack and repeat with the remaining oil and mixture.
Cut the pancakes into wedges or squares with a knife or kitchen scissors and serve hot with the dipping sauce.
